current_answer: Junior hiring has weakened in some AI-exposed work, but the cause is less certain than the headline. A four-country study of 2017–2025 hires and vacancies finds that the GenAI-exposure link to falling junior shares weakens sharply after accounting for remote-work exposure. Newer French administrative records still show a large entry-hiring gap through March 2026, and Anthropic reports a lower junior share of technical hires. None isolates how many jobs AI caused to disappear; broad U.S. tracking still finds no clear economy-wide footprint.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI shrink the junior job ladder?
catalogue_card.text: Junior hiring fell in AI-exposed work, but a four-country study finds the apparent AI link weakens sharply after accounting for remote-work exposure. The later French hiring gap remains; AI-caused job loss is not established.

summary: A four-country study finds that GenAI exposure loses much of its association with falling junior hiring shares when remote-work exposure is included.
French permanent hires of 21–29-year-olds still fell faster in the most AI-exposed occupations through March 2026; that later result is not explained by the four-country study.
Anthropic reports a lower junior share of technical hires at its own expanding firm; this is not an economy-wide job-loss count.
Broad U.S. tracking still finds no clear economy-wide AI labor-market footprint.
uncertainty: The remote-work study is observational and ends in 2025; it cannot rule out later or country-specific AI effects.
The French analysis is descriptive and its flows do not measure age-by-occupation employment stocks.
Anthropic is one rapidly growing firm reporting internal, non-audited records.
The Copilot studies use different firm samples and hiring denominators; neither establishes an economy-wide effect.
The adaptive-capacity study combines occupation-level exposure and transition proxies, not observed AI layoffs or realized reemployment.
Occupation averages conceal individual circumstances; future demand may change the ranking.
A new German journal abstract covers mostly pre-generative-AI adoption; its full methods were not accessible.
The sector study uses task exposure rather than observed AI deployment and adjusts a pre-trend in its automatable-task series.
The Argentine experiment took place outside workplaces and did not test actual job access or wages.
The Swedish AI-skill study covers 2014–2023 external hires and excludes ordinary chatbot use; its observational pay gap cannot identify a causal return to training.
The October tracker summary did not expose its full updated data vintage or detailed estimates in the page inspected.
freshness_note: Checked 22 October 2026. Remote work is a strong competing explanation in a four-country hiring study through 2025; newer French hiring flows remain unresolved.
